title: The constructive speech
summary: Build a two minute constructive that signposts its points, gives every point one claim, one reason and one real piece of evidence, and lands inside the timer both sides share.
materials: the 2 minute sand timer from week 1
index cards or a small notebook
a grown-up to hold the timer and listen without helping

steps.title: What a constructive is, and what it is not
steps.body:
Last week you met the shape of a formal debate: who speaks, in what order, and the timer sitting between the two sides like a referee both of you share. Today you learn the first speech in that shape, and it is the speech that decides most rounds.

A constructive builds. It is not an argument with anybody, because nobody has said anything yet. Its whole job is to put your case on the table so clearly that the judge can write it down while you are still talking.

Three things make it work.

Signposting. Give the judge the map before you walk it. I have two points. My first point is that the machine never gets tired. My second point is that the machine cannot tell whether the question it was given was a fair one. Then say my first point again when you actually get there. It sounds almost too obvious out loud, and that is exactly why it works: a judge taking notes can always find where you are.

One claim per point. A point that argues three things at once is a point nobody can write down. Pick the single sentence you want the judge to carry to the ballot, and make everything else in that point serve it.

An evidence slot in every point. After the claim and the reason there is a hole in your speech shaped like a fact, and it has to be filled with something that happened outside your own head: a number, a thing you built, a thing you watched, a thing you read. I think computers are usually right is not evidence. This week I submitted a program and the grader turned it down before it was correct, and the grader was right and I was wrong is evidence.

The timer is the referee, not the enemy. It runs the same for both sides. Finishing at one minute fifty with your best point landed beats being cut off at two minutes in the middle of a sentence. Learning to like the timer is part of the skill, not a punishment attached to it.

The motion this week: if a computer says it, you should believe it. You have spent this week watching a machine judge your own work, so you are carrying real evidence for both sides already.

steps.title: Write it on cards
steps.body:
Pick your side first, and pick it honestly. The side you actually believe today is the easier place to learn a new shape, and you will get plenty of chances to argue the other one later in the season.

Write the speech on cards, not in full sentences. The cards hold the map and your mouth fills in the words. Use this skeleton:

Card 1: the motion, your side, and the signpost. I have two points, then one short line naming each.

Card 2: point one. Claim, one sentence. Reason, one sentence starting with because. Evidence, the real thing that happened. Then one line linking the point back to the motion.

Card 3: point two, the same four parts.

Card 4: the close. No new material, just your two points said once more in about ten words.

Two rules while you write. Every evidence slot has to be filled before you stand up, and if you cannot fill one, that point is not ready and you swap it for a point you can actually back. And no point may need more than two sentences of setup, because setup eats the clock and no judge has ever scored setup.
checklist: I picked a side and can say in one sentence why I picked that one
My cards name both points before I argue either of them
Every point has a claim, a reason and a piece of evidence from outside my own head
No card is written out in full sentences, so I am talking and not reading

steps.title: Deliver it against the clock
steps.body:
A grown-up holds the 2 minute sand timer and turns it over the moment you start. They do not coach, interrupt or rescue you. When the sand runs out they say time, and you stop, even in the middle of a word.

Run one. Speak it. Whatever happens, happens, and nothing about it is a failure.

Then read what the clock told you. If you were cut off, something is too long, and it is almost never the evidence: it is the setup at the front of a point. Cut the setup, keep the proof. If you finished with thirty seconds to spare, one of your points is thin, and its evidence probably got mentioned instead of said properly.

Run two. Change the one thing the clock showed you, nothing else, and deliver it again. Run two is the one you record.

Two habits worth more than any clever line. Look up at the end of every point, at the person, not at your cards. And when you have a number, say it slowly and clearly, because a number said clearly is the part of a speech a judge writes down word for word.
checklist: Run one went all the way to the timer with no coaching and no rescue
I named the one thing the clock showed me and changed exactly that
Run two landed inside two minutes with both points finished
I looked up from my cards at the end of each point

steps.title: Record it
steps.prompt: Record run two of your constructive, start to finish, with the timer running. Then, still recording, answer the question of the week in your own words: is code you copied still yours? Say what changes if you tell people where it came from, and what changes if you do not.
